title: Passion Has a Secret No One Knows
intro: Al-Ukbari's heading tells the occasion: in 336 AH (947–948 CE) al-Mutanabbi was travelling from al-Ramla to Antioch and stopped at Tripoli, where Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Kayghalagh, egged on by three men of the Banu Haydara, asked him for a praise poem; the poet pleaded an oath not to praise anyone for a set time, and Ishaq held him there, watching the roads, until the time should run out. He wrote this satire instead and dictated it to someone he trusted; when the snow melted he rode out as if exercising his horse and made for Damascus, the horsemen and footmen Ibn Kayghalagh sent after him failed to catch him, and the poem came out. It opens with love and the poet's early grey hair, turns to maxims on human nature, then to Ibn Kayghalagh, and ends by praising Abu al-Asha'ir of the Hamdanids as the man who deserves praise. Al-Sahib ibn Abbad took twelve of its lines into his collection of al-Mutanabbi's proverbial verses, and Ibn Jinni judged that line 10 alone would have put the poet ahead of many of the modern poets.

translation: Passion has a secret no one can know:
I looked by chance and thought I would be safe.
1.sharh: No one can tell where love comes from in time to guard against it: he glanced at her by chance, sure he would escape, and did not. Ibn Jinni says the opening hints at what follows.

translation: Sister of the man who grapples horsemen in battle,
your brother, there, is gentler and kinder than you.
2.sharh: He tells the woman he loves that her brother, a hero who grapples enemy riders, is gentler in battle with his foes than she is with her lover. Ibn Jinni read a slur on the man satirised; al-Wahidi and al-Ma'arri reject it.

translation: The startling white on my parting alarmed you;
had white come first, the black would have alarmed you.
3.sharh: Whiteness itself is nothing to fear: had hair grown white first and darkened later, black would have alarmed her, as al-Wahidi explains. Al-Ma'arri adds that grey hair is disliked only because it announces the end of youth.

translation: If I could, I would unveil my youth:
grey hair before its time is a veil.
4.sharh: If he could, he would uncover his youth to show how young he is: grey hair that comes too early only veils it. Al-Ma'arri hears a complaint that grey hair has wronged him by coming too soon.

translation: I have seen what time brings, and I see
no white that kills and no black that protects.
5.sharh: Experience has taught him that white hair does not bring death nearer and black hair does not keep it off: old men live on and young men die. Al-Ma'arri reads it as advice not to dread greying.

translation: Worry wastes the stoutest body thin,
greys a boy's forelock and makes him old.
6.sharh: Care wears away the strongest body and greys and ages a boy before his time. Al-Barquqi notes that the poet is giving the reason for his own early grey: worry has whitened his hair, not the years.

translation: The man of reason is wretched amid plenty for his reason,
and the ignorant man is happy in misery.
7.sharh: The thinking man is unhappy even in comfort, because he weighs how things will end and knows that fortune turns; the ignorant man is happy in hardship, never looking ahead. Al-Wahidi sets a line of al-Buhturi's beside it.

translation: People have cast loyalty aside: a freed captive
forgets what was done for him, and the forgiver regrets it.
8.sharh: No one keeps faith any more: a freed prisoner forgets the kindness done him, and a man who pardons a wrong regrets it, because no one thanks him. Ibn Jinni objects that regretting a good deed is never commendable.

translation: Do not let an enemy's tears deceive you;
spare your youth from the enemy you would spare.
9.sharh: When an enemy is in your power, do not be moved by his tears; spare yourself rather than an enemy you pity, for if he gets the upper hand he will not pity you, as al-Wahidi explains.

translation: High honour is not safe from harm
until blood is shed on every side of it.
10.sharh: High honour is never safe from envious and hostile men until its owner kills them; then he is feared and left alone. Ibn Jinni wrote: “I swear by God, had al-Mutanabbi composed nothing but this line, it would have put him ahead of many of the modern poets.”

translation: The base among the mean, by his nature, harms
the man who is not as base and mean as he.
11.sharh: A mean, worthless man harms by his very nature anyone who is not mean and worthless like him, because the two have nothing in common, says al-Wahidi: the base are born to wrong the noble.

translation: Wrongdoing is in the nature of souls: if you find
a man of virtue, some cause keeps him from wrong.
12.sharh: Injustice is part of human nature: a decent man who wrongs no one is held back by something. Al-Ma'arri lists those who refrain for fear of God, those who cannot do wrong, and those who are ashamed to.

translation: It is an affliction to blame one who will not turn
from his folly, and to talk to one who cannot understand.
13.sharh: It is a misfortune to reproach a man who will not give up his ignorance, or to reason with one who does not understand. The man meant is Ibn Kayghalagh, described in the lines that follow.

translation: His eyelids never rest, as if his eyes
had been struck, or sour grapes crushed into them.
14.sharh: His eyelids never keep still, as though his eye had been hit or sour grape juice squeezed into it. Al-Wahidi says he is forever winking to beckon foreign louts; another commentary sees a defect in his eye.

translation: When he gestures as he talks, he is
a cackling monkey, or an old woman slapping her face.
15.sharh: He cannot speak plainly and waves his hands as he talks, like a cackling monkey or an old woman slapping her cheeks: a jibe at his ugly, twitching face, says al-Wahidi. Ibn al-Shajari reads “or” as leaving the choice of likeness open.

translation: You see him at his smallest when he speaks,
and he lies the most when he swears.
16.sharh: He looks most contemptible when he opens his mouth, because he stammers, and he lies most when he swears. Al-Wahidi reads the end as “most lying when swearing”; Ibn al-Shajari compares “a governor is at his most eloquent standing”.

translation: Abasement makes the abject man show love,
and fonder than he of the man he courts is the spotted snake.
17.sharh: An abject man shows love to whoever humbles him, since he can neither resist nor repay him; yet a snake is truer in love than he is. Al-Wahidi traces the thought to a line of Sudayf's.

translation: Some enmity brings you good,
and some friendship harms and hurts.
18.sharh: Not every enmity is bad nor every friendship good. Ibn Jinni explains: a base man's hostility shows that his nature is unlike yours, which is to your credit; his friendship shows that you are alike, which does you harm.

translation: You sent, in your folly, to ask me for praise:
Safra' is narrower than you; what could I claim?
19.sharh: Turning to Ibn Kayghalagh: he foolishly asked for praise, when even his mother Safra', for all that is said of her, is less contemptible than he, so nothing true can be said in his praise, as Ibn Jinni explains.

translation: How far you climbed beyond your worth,
and how near the stars seemed to you.
20.sharh: Asking for praise was overreaching: he thought he could reach the stars. The stars, says al-Wahidi, are the poet's verses, as far above such a man as the sky.

translation: You wanted what is Abu al-Asha'ir's alone:
praise belongs to the man who, visited, gives.
21.sharh: Ibn Kayghalagh wanted for himself the praise that belongs to Abu al-Asha'ir alone, for praise is earned by the man who receives his visitors with gifts. With this line the satire turns to praise of Abu al-Asha'ir.

translation: And to the man at whose door you stayed in disgrace:
you come near, your neck is struck, you are driven off.
22.sharh: Praise belongs to Abu al-Asha'ir, at whose door Ibn Kayghalagh waited in humiliation, slapped and shooed away whenever he came near. Al-Wahidi compares a line of Jarir's about envoys whose moustaches are plucked at the doors of kings.

translation: And to the man who scorns wealth though it is prized,
and leads an army vast in number.
23.sharh: Praise belongs to the man who gives money away as if it were nothing, though others hold it dear, and who leads a huge army. Al-Ukbari allows another reading: he scorns his wealth while he himself is honoured.

translation: And to the man who, when armoured champions meet in a tight place,
takes as his share the champion who wears a mark.
24.sharh: When warriors clash in the press of battle, he goes for the most famous fighter among them, not for the spoils. Al-Ukbari compares Abu Tammam's lions, who want the slain, not what they wore.

translation: Often he bends his spear in one horseman,
then turns and straightens it in another.
25.sharh: His thrust is so hard that his spear bends in the first man he strikes, and so quick that he straightens it in the next: a picture, says al-Barquqi, of how hard and fast he fights.

translation: His face shining, his heart bold,
his spear dark, his sword cutting through bone.
26.sharh: He fights with a bright face and a steady heart, a dark spear and a sword that never glances off. The Arabic says “the face, the heart”; al-Barquqi notes that each “the” stands for “his”.

translation: The deeds of those born of noble parents are noble,
and the deeds of those born of barbarians are barbarous.
27.sharh: Men act according to their birth: noble parents produce noble deeds, foreign stock mean ones. To the Arabs, says al-Wahidi, foreigners stood for meanness; al-Barquqi notes that the jibe is aimed at Ibn Kayghalagh, who was of Byzantine stock.

2.1.3-4.meaning: “The one who embraces horsemen”: a champion who grapples with enemy riders at close quarters.

2.2.2.meaning: There: in battle. Ibn Jinni took it as pointing to a place of shame.

3.1.2-3.meaning: “The alarming one of whiteness”: white hair, which startles whoever sees it. Al-Wahidi reports that Ibn Jinni read ra'iyat al-bayad, the first white hair to grow.

3.1.4.head: مَفرِق
3.1.4.meaning: Mafriq: the parting of the hair, the crown of the head. The editions have bi-aridi, “on my cheek”, where the beard grows.

3.2.1-2.meaning: “Even if it were”: law annaha with the hamza dropped for the metre.

5.2.1.head: يَقَق
5.2.1.meaning: Yaqaq: dazzling white; here white hair.

8.2.3.head: أَولى
8.2.3.meaning: Is given (a favour). One commentary reads yuli, “gives”.

9.2.5.head: رَحِمَ
9.2.5.meaning: “You pity”: an enemy you pity, with “him” understood.

11.1.2.head: القَليل
11.1.2.meaning: “The little one”: the paltry, contemptible man, not “few”.

12.1.3.head: شيمَة
12.1.3.meaning: Natures, inborn traits. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Jinni read “in the make of souls”.

13.2.2.head: جَهل
13.2.2.meaning: His ignorance, folly. Al-Wahidi, al-Ukbari and al-Barquqi read ghayyihi, “his error”.

14.1.1.head: جَفن
14.1.1.meaning: His eyelids: those of Ibn Kayghalagh, the man satirised, whose name comes in a line the reciter leaves out.

14.2.1.head: مَطروقَة
14.2.1.meaning: Struck. The editions have matrufa, “hit in the eye” so that it waters.

14.2.5.head: حِصرِم
14.2.5.meaning: Unripe green grapes, which are sour.

17.2.5.head: الأَرقَم
17.2.5.meaning: Arqam: a snake speckled black and white.

19.2.1.head: صَفراء
19.2.1.meaning: Safra': the satirised man's mother, say al-Wahidi and Ibn Jinni; one commentary makes her his wife.

20.2.5.head: النَّجم
20.2.5.meaning: The stars: the poet's verses, says al-Wahidi.

21.1.1.head: أَرادَ
21.1.1.meaning: You wanted. The editions have wa-arghta, “you sought”, which Ibn Jinni glosses “you sought and wanted”.

21.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Asha'ir: al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Hamdan, of the Hamdanid house, whom al-Mutanabbi praised in “Atuuraha li-kathrat al-ushshaq”.

22.2.3.head: أَخدَع
22.2.3.meaning: Your akhda'an: the two veins at the sides of the neck; striking them means a slap on the neck.

24.1.5.head: مَأزِق
24.1.5.meaning: Ma'ziq: a narrow place, hence the press of battle.

24.2.4.head: المُعلِم
24.2.4.meaning: The horseman who wears a champion's mark so that he is known in battle.

26.2.4.head: مُصَمِّم
26.2.4.meaning: Said of a sword that strikes bone and cuts through it.

27.2.4.head: الأَعجَم
27.2.4.meaning: A'ajim: non-Arabs; the Arabs called anyone who did not speak their language a'jam, whatever his people (al-Wahidi).
